To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
castration does not alter eicosanoid synthesis, but does decrease LHRH release from the ME of adult rats in vitro.
the absence of testosterone does not block the ability of eicosanoid or catecholamine agonists to stimulate LHRH release in vitro.

the absence of testosterone in the adult male rat does not block the release of Luteinizing Hormone Releasing Hormone (LHRH), which is stimulated by eicosanoids and catecholamines in vitro, nor does it affect the biosynthesis of prostaglandins and leucotrienes in the hypothalamus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of eicosanoid synthesis and release in the regulation of LHRH release from the ME of male rats in vitro.
the effect of long-term castration on the release of eicosanoid- and catecholaminergic-induced LHRH release from the ME of adult rats in vitro.
the role of eicosanoid mediators in the regulation of LHRH release in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
gonadal steroids have no effect on the synthesis or the release of LHH in vitro.
the absence of the gonads does not interfere with either the biosynthetic or the release mechanisms of eicosanoid or catecholamine stimulators of LHRH release by the ME.
the gonadal steroids have no effect on either the biosynthesis or the action of eicosoids on LHRH release in vitro.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stimulatory effect of gonadal steroids on the release of hypothalamic LHRH is mediated at the ME.
castration reduces the basal release of LHR H by the ME but that this effect is not mediated by a reduction in the synthesis of eicosanoid or catecholamine-stimulated LHRH release.
the ME is not a major target organ of gonadal steroid action.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the release of LHH from the ME of adult castrated rats is reduced by castration.
castration does not alter the stimulatory action exerted by PGE2 and catecholamines (NE and DA) on LHRH release.
castration reduces the absolute amounts of LHRH released under basal and stimulated conditions.
